newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire government says Kabila a puppet.
newsitem.headline: Zaire government says Kabila a puppet.

text.p: Zaire's government said on Thursday it considered rebel leader Laurent Kabila a puppet but was open to the idea of a regional conference provided all foreign troops left its territory.

"We do not understand how the United States can be pushing us to negotiate with Kabila after recognising that Zaire has been the victim of foreign aggression," Pascale Dema, prime minister Kengo wa Dondo's spokesman, told Reuters.
"We consider him a puppet," he said, referring to Kabila, who had talks in South Africa with President Nelson Mandela on Wednesday.

The Zairean government has repeatedly rejected the idea of talks with Kabila. "We are, however, open to the idea of a regional conference provided that the U.N. resolutions of February 19 calling for the withdrawal of foreign troops are applied," Dema said.
In South Africa, a senior official for the rebels said the movement was ready for talks with the government of President Mobutu Sese Seko to end Zaire's civil war but first wanted an agenda.
Bizima Karaha, foreign affairs spokesman for Kabila, told BBC radio in Pretoria there were no preconditions for the talks.
Mandela, who is trying to broker peace talks, spoke of progress on Thursday after talks with Mobutu's nephew and security adviser Honore Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba.
Zaire has consistently accused neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading in support of the Tutsi-led rebels, dismissing Kabila as a pawn in their hands.
Kabila, whose forces took up arms in October and have been pushing west despite a January 20 army counter-offensive, said on Wednesday he hoped negotiations could start soon.
Earlier, defence ministry officials said that the army had blocked rebel advances on Zaire's third city Kisangani and Kindu, a transport hub to the south.

A senior defence ministry official said the army had taken 50 prisoners on Wednesday when rebels attacked Bafwasende, 220 km (140 miles) north east of Kisangani, headquarters for military operations in the war zone.
There was no independent confirmation of the report but church sources in the area spoke of two rebels captured there earlier in the week.

Business sources in the region reported rebels bypassing Rwandan Hutu refugees in Tingi Tingi refugee camp and continuing on towards Kisangani. Rebels had camped near Pene-Katamba, 107 km (66 miles) south east of Kisangani, the sources said.
The army says it blocked a rebel advance on Kindu with an ambush on Tuesday and reinforced the town on Wednesday.
A regional military source told Reuters in Nairobi that the rebels were besieging the town but appeared to holding off attacking to allow civilians time to leave.
Zairean defence officials shrugged off suggestions that the rebels were besieging Kindu. "If they say they are at the doors of Kindu why don't they attack," one ministry official said.
There was no independent confirmation of either version.
Church sources in the region said they had no contact with Kindu on Thursday but that on Wednesday there was no sign of rebels near the town.
Opposition politicians in Kinshasa say rebel advances in the field give the government little alternative but to talk.
"The government has no choice. There is no other option but to negotiate before it is too late," the radical opposition Palmares newspaper said in a commentary.
